To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic stress, inflammation and colon cancer are interrelated via CRH-family members, and that this interrelationship is based on the modulation of a cascade involving multiple molecular signaling pathways.

chronic stress is involved in the development of CRC through the modulation of the CRH system, which is implicated in the regulation not only of the stress response but also of the inflammatory response.
chronic stress, via activation of a CRH-driven molecular cascade, is able to promote inflammation and colon carcinogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that link chronic stress to CRC, and with the development of novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of the disease.
the molecular crosstalk between stress and inflammation, with a particular focus on the CRH system, and its potential role in CRC.
the role of stress in the development of CRC and the molecular mechanisms that may be responsible for this effect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

chronic stress is a risk factor for CRC and other malignancies, through its ability to modulate inflammatory processes and, in parallel, the expression of CRH-family molecules, which are known to be involved in tumorigenesis.
chronic stress, inflammation and CRC are tightly interconnected, via a CRH-driven molecular crosstalk.
chronic stress, via the CRH system, may be involved in the development of CRC by promoting chronic inflammation, and that the CRH system may serve as a potential therapeutic target in CRC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

chronic stress is a major risk factor for the occurrence of CRC and that this risk can be modulated by the expression of CRH-family neuropeptides and their receptors in the brain and peripheral tissues.
stress and inflammation are closely linked, and the CRH system is one of the main regulators that mediate the crosstalk between these processes

stress, through the CRH system, may be involved in the regulation of the inflammatory response, and in the development of cancer, and that this may be mediated, in part, by a crosstalk between the brain and the periphery, which is orchestrated by the CRH system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stress, through the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, may promote inflammation and cancer development, via CRH-family members.
the CRH system is a potential molecular target for the prevention and/or treatment of CRC, which is currently being explored.
stress-induced inflammation, via CRH, may be a potential therapeutic target to treat CRC.
